newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Mass slaying leaves six dead in New Zealand.
newsitem.headline: Mass slaying leaves six dead in New Zealand.

text.p: A gunman went on a shooting rampage in a New Zealand town on Saturday, killing six people, including one woman, and seriously wounding up to five others in another mass murder to shatter the country's tranquil image.

Police arrested the suspected gunman after finding him naked and unarmed in farmland close to the scene of the slayings in the small North Island town of Raurimu, near the active volcano Mount Ruapehu.
Police said the suspect was 24 years old, against earlier reports that he was 50, and might have been related to some of the dead and wounded. They said he was believed to be a local resident.
The killer was believed to have committed the murders with a 12-gauge shotgun at around 9.00 a.m. (2000 GMT Friday).
Wanganui Acting District Commander Jeff Holloway said police took the suspect into custody shortly before midday (2300 GMT). They were still trying to identify the dead.

"The victims have not yet been properly identified. We don't know all the names as yet. We believe that a number of them at least are residents and may be related to the suspect," he told a news conference.
Police were also searching the bush for more victims.
"A scene search is under way. There is a possibility of further victims, but that's to be confirmed," a spokesman said.
The wounded were ferried by helicopters to hospitals in the district, he said. Raurimu was evacuated after police were notified of the shooting.
Helicopter pilot Guy Beange described the scene as "like Vietnam", with police and helicopters everywhere.
Beange flew one of the wounded to hospital and said a young man was flown to the hospital with a gunshot wound to the head. Two other people were taken to hospital by ambulance.
Saturday's slaying is the fifth mass slaughter in the 1990s that has shocked the country and undermined its image as a green and peaceful place.
In 1990, 13 people were killed by a young man in the hamlet of Aromana, near Dunedin in the south of the South Island. The police shot the gunman David Gray dead after a seige.
In May, 1992, 64-year-old farmer Brian Schlaepfer shot or stabbed six members of his family before killing himself with a shotgun at Pukekohe, near the northern city of Auckland.
The following month, an unemployed 25-year-old man stabbed or bludgeoned to death seven relatives including five children in the quiet rural town of Masterton, north of Wellington.

Then in 1994 a family of two parents and three children were shot dead with a rifle. Son David Bain was convicted for the mass murders but protested his innocence contending the father carried out the murders before committing suicide.

The series of massacres have traumatised New Zealand's 3.5 million people who used to take pride in the relatively low rate of violence. But violent crime has been on the increase for a number of years.
After the Aramona massacre, the government moved to tighten gunlaws and prohibit the sale of military-style assault rifles, which had been freely available.

But the laws did not come under the kind of scrutiny witnessed in Australia after the Port Arthur massacre of 35 people or in Britain after the Dunblane killing of 16 children and their teacher last year.
Anti-gun lobbyists believe New Zealand gun laws, which licence people rather than guns and still allow the possession of semi-automatic guns, are too lax.
